newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuania's Vagnorius says litas regime to go slowly.
newsitem.headline: Lithuania's Vagnorius says litas regime to go slowly.

text.p: Gediminas Vagnorius, Lithuania's prime minister-designate, said on Monday his government would gradually scrap the country's tough currency regime and unpeg the local currency, the litas, from the dollar.

Vagnorius told Reuters in an interview that the country would speed up privatisation and encourage investment. The currency regime, called currency board and introduced in April 1994 with the blessing from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), bars the central bank from using the exchange or interest rates as monetary policy tools.
Instead, the bank guarantees that it will maintain one U.S. dollar in its reserves for every four litas in circulation, freezing the exchange rate at that level.
The arrangement has helped curb inflation and restored confidence in the litas, but the Homeland Union has criticised it for choking off exports.
"We are firm on the issue of abolishing the currency board, but this measure should be gradually implemented and take from one to two years," Vagnorius told Reuters.
"Meanwhile, we will re-establish a strong central bank with all of its functions...to enable it to reduce both inflation and interest rates," he said.
Both issues featured prominently in the right-wing Homeland Union's campaing ahead of its sweeping victory in parliamentary elections last week.

But Vagnorius' post-election vows of a hasty exit from the currency board system drew a rebuke from the International Monetary Fund, which calls the system the lynch-pin of the country's transition to a market economy.
His suggestion that the currency would be allowed to depreciate along with the inflation rate sparked fears of devaluation and a run on the dollar in local banks.
The IMF said last week it would not support a rapid dismantling of the system.
After meeting with an IMF mission last Wednesday, Vagnorius backed down from a plan to phase the currency board out quickly at the start of 1997.
The IMF and other analysts credit the currency board for keeping the litas stable, reining in inflation, and inspiring investor confidence in Lithuania's emerging market.
Inflation has fallen in Lithuania from an annual rate of almost 1,200 percent in 1992 to over 23 percent in September.
But the Homeland Union argue the system has strangled exports because, they say, litas became gradually overvalued.
The party was strongly backed by the Confederation of Lithuanian Industrialists, who have lobbied hard for a devaluation in a bid to make their exports more competitive.
"If we keep the currency board forever, our foreign trade deficit could grow and this could spark panic in our financial markets," Vagnorius said.
He said his government would hasten the privatization process, a key area where Lithuania is viewed as something of a straggler.
Many small and medium-sized enterprises have passed into the private sector but a number of large firms and the energy, telecommunications and transport sectors remain firmly in state hands.
"We will sell large state-run enterprises in open auctions, organized by the state privatization agency. These will include Lithuanian Gas and the Mazeikiu oil refinery," Vagnorius said.
"We will not tax investment and will reduce the value added tax from 18 percent to 14 percent," he added.
